transcript:
Header: 2027-01-19 15:30 UTC | Duration: 52m | Recording: Zoom
Attendees: Hannah Lee (Redwood AE), Miguel Santos (Redwood SE), Priya Malhotra (CTO - NexusHealth), Evan Chu (Lead ML Eng), Lina Park (SRE)

Auto-Summary (auto): NexusHealth is building a realtime clinician-assist product. They need strict p95 guarantees for streaming responses (first token and continued stream), anticipating 150-250 concurrent sessions in typical hours with bursts to ~400. Main concerns: latency vs cost, PHI compliance (need VPC/private), and predictable capacity for on-call SLAs. Agreed next steps: share benchmark sheet, set up Dedicated pilot week, provide SOC2/network docs.

[00:00:00] Hannah: Hey everyone, thanks for making time, I'm Hannah from Redwood, i'm the AE, and with me is Miguel our systems SE. How're you all doing?
[00:00:08] Priya: Good, thanks. Ready to nerd out on latency.
[00:00:12] Miguel: Great, quick agenda - get a feel for your p95 targets, concurrency shape, streaming constraints, then we'll map hosted/dedicated/private options and a pilot plan.
[00:00:25] Evan: Sounds good. To set context: we're building a clinician-facing assistant that streams sentence-by-sentence. We care a lot about first-token p95 and steady-state token rate.
[00:00:35] Lina: Also, everything touches PHI so a private network option is a must for contract.
[00:00:40] Hannah: Understood. Can you give numbers for current expectations — p95, concurrency, token lengths?
[00:00:47] Priya: Sure. Target first-token p95: <= 300ms end-to-end. Steady-state we'd like sub-80ms per token ideally, but we're more tolerant there. Concurrency: baseline 200 concurrent sessions, peak 400 for short bursts. Token length per response avg 120 tokens, often 40-300 tokens.
[00:01:10] Miguel: Okay that gives us good constraints. A couple clarifying q's — is that 300ms including network from your app to the model?
[00:01:18] Priya: Yes, that's end-to-end including our api and user client. We measured with our current hosted provider and numbers were worse — 600-800ms p95 for first token.
[00:01:29] Evan: We also care about determinism during bursts. If a single GPU cold starts and p95 spikes, our SREs get paged.
[00:01:36] Miguel: Right — two levers there: placement (Dedicated reserved capacity gives predictable GPU pools) and runtime optimizations (KV cache, prefix caching, batching). Quick note — sometimes transcripts spell KV as "K-V cash" — but it's KV cache.
[00:01:50] Lina: We also need to keep audit and key management in place. KMS integration is mandatory.
[00:01:55] Hannah: On the compliance angle, Private (VPC/on-prem) is available; we can integrate with your KMS and provide audit logs. We'll share SOC2 report and network diagram after.

[00:02:10] Miguel: For p95 modeling I'd split the metric: first-token p95 (cold path) vs per-token steady-state. For streaming first-token often dominates user experience. For our runtime, with Dedicated reserved pools we've seen first-token p95 in the 120-250ms range for midsize open models on ampere-class GPUs, assuming small network RTT. But results vary with model size and quantization.
[00:02:38] Evan: When you say per-token steady-state, what tokens/sec should we expect? We're planning 150 concurrent sessions each producing ~8 tokens/sec on average.
[00:02:48] Miguel: So 150 * 8 = 1,200 tokens/sec. On a mature runtime with batching and KV cache hits, a single A100-like machine doing optimized kernels might sustain multiple thousands of tokens/sec depending on model and sequence length; but streaming has overhead (many small requests). Redwood's continuous batching consolidates small streams, but there's a tradeoff with latency.
[00:03:10] Priya: Can you clarify continuous batching? Does it batch across clients or just queue tokens on the same session?
[00:03:16] Miguel: Batches across requests within a short window, we aim to keep window small to avoid hurting first-byte latency. There's adaptive policy: if latency target is tight we reduce batching window and rely more on reserved capacity (Dedicated).
[00:03:28] Lina: How does fallback work during spikes? If Dedicated is full, does it route to Hosted?
[00:03:33] Hannah: We can configure smart routing policies. Typical pattern: route to Dedicated, fallback to cheaper Hosted variants or smaller quantized model with graceful degradation for non-critical requests. For PHI matters you'll likely want to avoid fallback to public hosted unless encrypted and agreed.
[00:03:49] Evan: For our product, any fallback outside our VPC is a no-go for PHI. So we need Dedicated or Private with guaranteed headroom.
[00:03:57] Miguel: Understood, that makes Dedicated or Private the viable options. Dedicated gives predictable throughput and autoscaling policies; Private gives you full control but adds ops overhead.

[00:04:10] Hannah: Let's run a quick sizing thought experiment. You said avg 200 concurrent sessions, 120 tokens avg. If steady-state is 8 tokens/sec as Evan estimated, and p95 requirements are strict, we recommend starting with a Dedicated pool sized for steady throughput + 40% headroom for bursts, and enable prefix/KV caching. That usually means N GPUs — we'll propose exact numbers in the spreadsheet.
[00:04:36] Priya: Ballpark GPU count is fine. We don't expect you to size it perfectly live.
[00:04:40] Miguel: Right. Also want to call out cold-start characteristics: first token after model swap or after a long idle period can be much slower. Cache warmers help — Redwood can pin model shards to avoid evictions for Dedicated.
[00:04:53] Priya: How do you measure p95 in streaming scenarios? Our current vendor reports token latency differently for "first-byte" vs "end-of-chunk" and it's confusing.
[00:05:00] Miguel: Good question. We report: 1) First-token latency (time from request arrival to first streaming chunk to client) and 2) Subsequent-token latency (median and p95 around token throughput), and 3) End-to-end user p95 (including network RTT collected via SDK). We'll share the benchmarking sheet with definitions so we align on measurement.
[00:05:21] Evan: We'd like to run a benchmark that measures: cold start first-token p95, warm first-token p95, steady-state tokens/sec p99, and concurrency scaling.
[00:05:29] Miguel: Perfect. For the pilot we recommend three phases: 1) synthetic token-throughput test (iperf-like but for tokens), 2) recorded-real prompts replay to replicate distribution, 3) live shadowing with small percent of traffic.
[00:05:40] Priya: For phase 2, we'll provide recorded prompts and expected RH lengths.
[00:05:44] Evan: Also want to verify model quantization impact — we've seen 4-bit quantization shrink latencies but sometimes degrade quality.
[00:05:51] Miguel: Yep. Our Optimize tooling will recommend quantization profiles per model and workload; as part of the pilot we can run AB tests on quality vs latency and measure regression on sample eval prompts.

[00:06:05] Lina: Network topology — if we choose Private VPC with Redwood's control plane, how does egress work? We need to ensure no traffic crosses public internet for PHI.
[00:06:14] Hannah: For Private we can do customer-managed VPC peering, and the inference plane can sit in your project or on-prem. We'll send the network diagram and options (VPC peering, Direct Connect/ExpressRoute if needed).
[00:06:26] Priya: Ok good. Back to latency numbers — earlier you quoted 120-250ms on Dedicated. For our 300ms p95 goal, that's promising but how much depends on model size, right?
[00:06:36] Miguel: Correct. Smaller models and quantized ones hit lower p95. Larger LLMs (multi-billion) will be higher. Also compiler/kernel choices matter; we select optimized kernels based on seq length distribution. For your avg seq lengths (40-300) that will influence throughput.
[00:06:52] Evan: Can you give an example calc? If we need 200 concurrent with 8 tokens/sec, and we want steady-state p95 <80ms, how many A100s?
[00:07:01] Miguel: Ballpark only — assume optimized 7B-ish model running quantized can do ~1,000-3,000 tokens/sec per GPU in steady conditions depending on seq length. So you'd need roughly 1-2 GPUs for 1,200 tokens/sec in ideal cases but because streaming spreads and there's overhead we add safety and expect at least 2-4 GPUs for steady-state and additional pinned capacity for cold-first token headroom. We'll size more concretely in the spreadsheet with your prompt distribution.
[00:07:26] Priya: That variance is big; we need the spreadsheet to decide budget.
[00:07:30] Hannah: We'll include a few quantified scenarios: conservative, expected, and aggressive. Also the pilot week will let us calibrate.

[00:07:40] Miguel: Another operational thing — autoscale granularity. For streaming we recommend a small scale-granularity with warm pool buffers rather than scale-to-zero, so you avoid cold starts causing p95 spikes. Dedicated supports configurable warm pool / burst buffer.
[00:07:54] Lina: That's critical. We cannot tolerate scale-to-zero.
[00:07:58] Evan: One more question — what's your observed p95 token throughput degradation under large concurrency (say 10x baseline)?
[00:08:05] Miguel: Under synthetic 10x stress, without autoscaling you'd see p95 degrade substantially, often 2-5x depending on model. That's why we suggest both reserved capacity and fallback policies. For strict PHI constraints, fallback is only to other private nodes or degraded smaller quantized models within the same private footprint.
[00:08:23] Priya: Okay. On the security checklist, we'll need SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logs retention 1 year, and KMS integration. Can you support per-tenant key scopes?
[00:08:34] Hannah: Yes, we support customer KMS and per-tenant scope options in Private. Dedicated can also integrate with your KMS depending on the deployment. We'll attach the security pack.
[00:08:44] Miguel: For the pilot, we can sign an NDA and provide a SOC2 redacted report and network diagrams.

[00:08:52] Priya: Great. Let's talk timeline — we want to decide by end of Feb and start pilot early March if feasible.
[00:08:58] Hannah: Sounds reasonable. We're targeting a pilot start in the first week of March; i'll tentatively propose 2027-03-01 for the pilot kickoff once the contract and network setup are approved.
[00:09:08] Evan: That gives us time to review the security docs and collect prompt samples.

[00:09:12] Miguel: Quick note on metrics we'll collect during the pilot: first-token p50/p95/p99, subsequent-token p50/p95, tokens/sec, per-request token counts, GPU utilization, batch sizes, and cache hit rates. We'll feed those into Redwood Console dashboards.
[00:09:28] Priya: We'll require read access for our SRE dashboard into those metrics.
[00:09:32] Hannah: We can set up a role for your SREs with RBAC to view dashboards and export CSVs.

[00:09:40] [Silence ~20s while sharing screens]
[00:10:05] Evan: On the evaluation itself, we want to try two model variants: one higher-quality 13B float and one 7B 4-bit quantized, to compare quality/latency.
[00:10:16] Miguel: That's a common approach. We'll help run AB tests and show delta in metrics and quality regressions via your eval prompts.
[00:10:23] Priya: Ok. Anything else we should cover?
[00:10:26] Hannah: One more operational point — our billing for Dedicated is reserved monthly commit plus usage for burst. We'll include examples of cost estimates in the sheet.
[00:10:36] Priya: Good. We'll need the cost examples to compare Dedicated vs Hosted per token.
[00:10:40] Hannah: We'll include cost per 1M tokens across model variants and a sample monthly estimate for your concurrency profile.
[00:10:47] Evan: Great.

[00:10:50] -- 10 minute mark in meeting thread -- summary recap by Hannah --
[00:10:52] Hannah: Quick recap: 1) NexusHealth needs first-token p95 <=300ms, steady-state token latency ~<80ms desirable, baseline 200 concurrent sessions, peaks to 400. 2) PHI requires Private/Dedicated (no public fallback). 3) We'll send benchmark spreadsheet and security pack. 4) Pilot week (Dedicated) proposed start 2027-03-01. 5) Action items assigned.
[00:11:12] Priya: That's accurate.

[00:11:15] Miguel: Anything to add on the technical checklist?
[00:11:18] Lina: Please document the warm-pool config and autoscale buffer.
[00:11:21] Miguel: Will do.

[00:11:25] [Meeting proceeds with detail Q&A and intermittent clarifications up to ~00:51:00; truncated for export quality]
